name: SIP32510DT-T1-GE3
title: SiP32510: load switch with controlled output slew, 1.2 V to 5.5 V, in TSOT23-6
summary: A single high-side load switch for rails from 1.2 V to 5.5 V, built round an n-channel pass device. On-resistance stays near 44 mΩ from 1.8 V to 5 V, and the output ramps up over a controlled 1.6 ms (typical, 3.3 V) after a 0.4 ms delay, which holds down inrush into large load capacitance. When off it draws under 1 µA, blocks current flowing back from the output (also with no input applied) and pulls the output down through about 217 Ω. The EN input works from low-voltage logic with no level shifter; the part comes in TSOT23-6 as SiP32510DT-T1-GE3.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit
circuits.description: The switch sits between a supply rail and a load. A 4.7 µF capacitor on the input holds the rail up against the inrush step, a 0.1 µF capacitor on the output handles load transients, and a logic signal on EN turns the output on and off.
notes: U1.IN stands for pins 5 and 6, U1.OUT for pins 1 and 2.

where.dropout voltage: voltage from IN to OUT, sensed with Kelvin connections at the pins

operation.text: The pass element is an n-channel MOSFET on the high side. Enabling the part turns the gate on at a set rate, so the output ramps instead of stepping and inrush current stays low; once the switch is fully on, gate-source voltage is held at a fixed level, which keeps on-resistance flat across the supply range. Turn-on delay is 0.4 ms typical and rise time 1.6 ms typical, about 2 ms in total. Output capacitance has little influence on the ramp time.

td(on) runs from EN crossing 50 % on its rising edge to OUT reaching 10 %; tr from 10 % to 90 % of OUT; t(on) from the 50 % EN point to OUT reaching 95 %. td(off) runs from EN falling through 50 % to OUT dropping to 90 %.

With the switch off, a blocking circuit stops current flowing from OUT back into IN whenever the output sits above the input. It still works with the input at 0 V. Reverse leakage is under 2 µA; the specified limit at VOUT = 5 V, VIN = 0 V is 10 µA max.
An internal detector compares VOUT with VIN. When VOUT rises 0.8 V above VIN, a pull-down of about 1 kΩ connects EN to GND and forces the switch off.
While EN is inactive, the output is pulled to ground through RPD, 217 Ω typical and 280 Ω max at 25 °C.

EN accepts TTL and CMOS levels and needs no level-shifting from low-voltage logic. EN may be driven above IN as long as it stays within its absolute maximum rating. The input thresholds scale with VIN.

No input capacitor is required for the switch to work. To limit dips on the supply from the inrush current, a 2.2 µF ceramic capacitor between IN and GND, close to the pins, is recommended; a larger value reduces the dip further. Ceramic types are preferred because they tolerate surge current from stiff sources such as batteries.

The switch runs without an output capacitor, but 0.1 µF or more from OUT to GND is recommended for load transients; it also keeps parasitic inductance from driving VOUT below ground at turn-off. Neither the dielectric type nor the ESR is constrained.

Layout and assembly limit the switch to 3 A continuous. Below that, the usable current is set by package dissipation and by RDS(on) at the ambient temperature. The 150 °C/W figure assumes the IN and OUT pins are tied into copper areas that act as heat sinks; tracks and vias on IN and OUT should be sized for the full continuous current. Exceeding the computed current heats the die and can damage the part.

On the evaluation board at 25 °C, the part carries 5 A pulses of 1 ms repeated every 4.6 ms, with 180 mA flowing between pulses, without harm. With the switch already enabled, it tolerates a single inrush of up to 12 A for 100 µs at 25 °C, as when a large capacitive load is connected.

Keep every track short to cut inductance and parasitics. Place the input capacitor at the IN pins and the output capacitor at the OUT pins. Wide IN, OUT and GND tracks lower the thermal impedance from case to ambient.

Sense the IN-to-OUT drop with Kelvin connections taken right at the pins, so the voltage lost along the current-carrying tracks does not enter the reading, and measure the load current with an ammeter. On the evaluation board J5 (IN-S) and J6 (OUT-S) are the sense points.
